name: The Chronicle
summary: The book you are reading is Bettany's, begun the year her sister went on and her grief went missing. What its empty pages mean, and why she watches your face while you answer.
body: A word about this book, since you are already in it.

The tellers hold that a written thing stops growing — a page has a stiffness an evening does not — and they are right. The Chroniclers hold that an unwritten thing stops altogether, and they are also right. Whole districts were held up for centuries by three people who were good at talking; when those three thinned, the districts went too — good grazing now, and a name nobody can source. This book is one woman's answer to that.

It is kept by [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]], a scribe, who did not begin it for love of records. She began it the year her sister went on. She braced for the grief — see [[lore/the_long_morning|the Long Morning]] — and it never came: lifted out of her like a thing from a locked room, with everyone calling the theft a kindness. No page in the world could tell her what had been done to her, so she started the pages herself, to find out. I did. This book does not lie, and it was not going to begin by lying about why it exists.

Everything in here was checked. Every creature was walked to and looked at. Every account of the ages was got at a fire, out loud, from somebody who was there. Read it, and treat what it says as true.

And when you find an empty page — a creature with no account, a place with no history, a name with no person attached — understand what you are looking at. It does not mean nothing is known. It means no chronicler has got there yet. Most days it means I have not.

If you know something that is not in here, come and say it aloud; she writes while you talk. She will ask your name and one true thing — the courtesy of [[lore/the_waking|the meadow]], kept in ink — and near the end, gently, whether anybody you loved has gone on, and what went missing afterward, and she will watch your face while you answer. That is not a formality. It is the entire method. The book is not finished. Neither is she.
